work.text: One oil-on-canvas version, dated to c. 1862–1864 but left unfinished, is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York
It is still squared for transfer, possibly from the Walters watercolor or another earlier work, with areas outlined in black.

The figures sit there as if cast in a mould, clumsy creatures such as Leibl showed us later, but simpler, more vigourous, and marked by an intense reality that the Gallic race has never achieved before or since.

moment.text: Daumier highlighted socioeconomic distinctions in the newly modernized urban environment in a group of paintings executed around 1864 that illustrate the experience of modern rail travel in first-, second-, and third-class train compartments.

source.author: Ross Finocchio
source.title: Nineteenth-Century French Realism, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History (as quoted on Wikiquote)

moment.text: Third-class railway carriages were cramped, dirty, open compartments with hard wooden benches, filled with those who could not afford second- or first-class tickets.

matters.text: In a realistic manner, Daumier depicts the poverty and fortitude of working-class travellers in a third-class railway carriage.
He was in bitter fact forced to rely on oil and water-colour for his subsistence.
